item.title: ICYMI: AMD slides 8% as short seller Hunterbrook ties its firmware to a blacklisted Chinese firm
item.description:
The allegations add a legal and regulatory overhang to a stock already hit by tighter US export licensing this month. Commerce’s response, or silence, is now the key variable. The China and Singapore revenue figures give bears a concrete number to point to, which could keep pressure on AMD even without any enforcement action. For the wider sector, a second short-seller campaign on China ties raises the risk premium on US chipmakers with large Asian sales, adding to the selling already hitting Asian chip stocks. Any sign of a BIS inquiry would be a fresh catalyst.

---

Earlier:

  • US approved nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China. Raises more questions than answers.

--- A short seller has put AMD’s China exposure in the spotlight, but by its own admission it hasn’t shown that any law was broken.

Summary:

  • AMD shares fell as much as 11% on Thursday and closed about 8% lower after Hunterbrook published a short report
  • Hunterbrook alleges IEIT Systems, blacklisted in March 2025, built at least six newer versions of AMD firmware into server updates
  • It says it cannot establish how IEIT obtained the code, whether a licence existed or that any export violation occurred
  • Hunterbrook’s investment arm is short AMD
  • AMD says the claims misrepresent its business and that it complies with US export laws
  • Hunterbrook says China and Hong Kong accounted for about 22% of AMD’s fiscal 2025 revenue

AMD shares fell as much as 11% on Thursday and closed about 8% lower after short seller Hunterbrook published a report alleging that a Chinese server maker on a US government blacklist has continued to use newer versions of the chipmaker’s software. Hunterbrook’s investment arm disclosed a short position in AMD, meaning it profits if the shares fall.

The report, titled “AMD has its own China problem,” centres on IEIT Systems, an arm of China’s Inspur Group. The Commerce Department added IEIT to its Entity List in March 2025 over its role in China’s supercomputer programme. Hunterbrook says IEIT has since built at least six newer versions of AMD’s startup firmware into server updates. The most recent was an update dated October 19, 2026, which contained firmware AMD released in July. It also says firmware posted by three other server companies, including Aivres, is nearly identical to IEIT’s, and points to corporate links between them.

Hunterbrook argues that software updates can count as exports under US rules, citing a recent enforcement settlement in which each post-listing update was treated as a separate violation. But it is careful about what it cannot show. It says it does not know how IEIT obtained the code or whether anyone held a licence, and that its findings do not establish an export violation. The Commerce Department has not commented.

AMD rejected the report. “The claims misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships,” a spokesperson said. The company added that it complies with US export control laws, maintains rigorous compliance processes across its global operations and remains focused on its customers.

For investors, the bigger question is China exposure. Citing AMD’s filings, Hunterbrook says billings to customers in China and Hong Kong were about $7.8 billion in fiscal 2025, roughly 22% of total revenue of about $35 billion, with a further $4.3 billion billed to Singapore. Singapore is among the countries covered by a new US licensing rule aimed at stopping advanced chips from reaching China through third countries. Hunterbrook also argues that AMD’s plan to grow data center AI revenue by more than 80% a year rests on the very chips facing tighter restrictions.

The report lands in a difficult month for US chipmakers. AMD had already fallen sharply in mid-November as Washington tightened export licensing, and Nvidia is facing its own short-seller scrutiny over China ties. With US lawmakers also releasing data this week on AI chip approvals for Chinese firms, the political pressure for stricter controls shows little sign of easing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Some analysts now see BoJ rates at 2.5% by mid-2027, despite slower underlying inflation
item.description:
A 2.5% BoJ path is far from priced, so the forecast is more a marker of upside risk than a market mover. If the coming months show underlying inflation turning higher, front-end JGB yields would be the first to reprice, with the yen likely to follow. The view also raises the stakes for the BoJ’s December 18 statement and Ueda’s press conference, where any hint of a faster pace would carry weight. With energy and imported costs feeding producer prices, oil and USD/JPY remain the key inputs to watch.

---

October’s slower underlying inflation hasn’t deterred the BoJ hawks: some forecasters now see rates at 2.5% by mid-2027, double today’s level.

Summary:

  • Some analysts expect a sharp acceleration in Japan’s inflation excluding fresh food and energy, despite October’s slowdown to 2.2% from 2.4%
  • They see further room for goods inflation and say producer prices point to faster food price rises
  • Some now expect the BoJ policy rate to reach 2.5% by mid-2027, up from earlier calls of around 2%
  • That would take five quarter-point hikes from today’s 1.25%, far faster than consensus
  • A Reuters poll shows 86% expect a hike to 1.50% in December and nearly 60% see 1.75% by end-March
  • Fresh food and briefly reduced utility subsidies lifted October’s headline reading to 2.3%

Some analysts are making a far more aggressive case for Bank of Japan tightening than the market, arguing that October’s slower underlying inflation reading is a pause rather than a turning point.

Japan’s core-core index, which excludes fresh food and energy and is closely watched by the BoJ, slowed to 2.2% in October from 2.4%. One camp of forecasters argues that a sharp acceleration in that measure is still likely over the coming months. They see further room for inflation in other industrial products, a broad category of manufactured goods, and say producer price data point to faster food inflation ahead. October’s producer prices rose 7.1% year on year, beating forecasts. Oil, chemicals, steel and utility costs climbed, and a weak yen pushed up import costs. Companies are still passing those costs on to consumers.

On that basis, some analysts now expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate to 2.5% by the middle of 2027. That marks a big step up from the same camp’s call only a month ago for a peak of around 2%, which was itself seen as above consensus. The pace is the sticking point. The BoJ has settled into a roughly quarterly rhythm of quarter-point hikes, moving in June and September and widely expected to act again in December. At that pace, the policy rate would reach about 2% by mid-2027. Getting to 2.5% from today’s 1.25% would require a hike at every one of the five meetings between December and June, or a larger move along the way. That would be a clear break from the steady approach the bank has followed so far.

The mainstream view is more measured. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, and nearly 60% expect 1.75% by the end of March. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the bank expects to keep raising rates. He flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target, but he has given no sign of an accelerated path.

There are also reasons for caution in the October data. Headline inflation rose to 2.3%, its highest in nearly a year. That was driven partly by a sharp increase in fresh food prices and by energy costs after the government briefly scaled back utility subsidies. Those subsidies are expected to return over the winter, which could take some heat out of headline readings in the coming months.

The debate matters for the yen. A BoJ path toward 2.5% would narrow the rate gap with the US far more quickly than markets expect, offering support for a currency trading near 160 per dollar. If underlying inflation instead stays around 2%, the gradual path priced by most economists looks more likely, and the yen would remain reliant on intervention warnings.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US approved nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China. Raises more questions than answers.
item.description:
The disclosure adds to political pressure for tighter China chip rules, a risk for Nvidia and AMD’s China revenue at a time when AI and semiconductor shares are already being sold hard across Asia. Nvidia saying it has stopped H200 shipments limits the near-term earnings hit, but any formal tightening would also weigh on Chinese AI developers’ access to computing power. Hong Kong-listed Tencent, Alibaba and Baidu are the most exposed names on the Chinese side. The story also keeps Washington’s broader export-control push in focus, including reported plans to curb advanced chip exports to parts of Southeast Asia.

---

Washington’s own licensing data show it cleared hundreds of thousands of AI chips for Chinese firms, including military-listed ones, handing China hawks fresh ammunition just as Nvidia says it has stopped shipping.

Summary:

  • The Commerce Department approved about 880,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chip shipments to Chinese firms from December 2025 to May 2026
  • Approvals included 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon’s military-linked list
  • Companies had sought licences for more than 3.4 million chips
  • It is unclear how many approved chips were actually delivered, and Nvidia says it has stopped shipping H200s to China
  • Commerce says licensing follows a January 2026 rule with extra national security requirements
  • The House committee called the release the most detailed public disclosure under the 2018 Export Control Reform Act

The US Commerce Department approved shipments of about 880,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, according to licensing data released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The approvals covered Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X. They included 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies appear on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed firms, and together they account for just over 30% of the approved total. Companies had sought permission to ship more than 3.4 million chips over the period, so roughly a quarter of requested volumes were approved.

It is not clear how many of the approvals turned into actual deliveries. Nvidia said the licences came with strict conditions and limited volumes and that “we have since stopped shipping H200s to China.” AMD said it complies with US export control laws. Reuters reported in May that about 10 Chinese companies had been cleared to buy the H200 but no deliveries had been made. A Commerce official later told the committee that shipments had begun but there had been very few.

The Commerce Department said its H200 licensing follows a January 2026 rule that adds significant national security requirements for applicants, allowing case-by-case review rather than a presumption of denial. Critics are unconvinced. A former US official who specialises in US-China technology policy called the share going to military-listed firms astonishing and questioned whether Commerce had carried out a serious security review.

The release is unusual. Committee Chair Brian Mast described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 expanded Commerce’s powers over sensitive technology exports. It comes as the Trump administration faces closer scrutiny of its China chip policy following reports involving former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, which have revived calls in Washington for a tougher stance.

The policy backdrop has swung sharply. The Biden administration restricted Chinese access to advanced AI chips over concerns they would strengthen China’s military and erode the US lead in AI. President Trump reversed course in December 2025, allowing Nvidia to ship the H200 to China. With pressure building on both sides of the political divide, investors will watch for any move to tighten licensing again. That would weigh on chipmakers’ China revenue and on Chinese tech firms’ access to advanced computing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China holds loan prime rates for an 18th month as the overnight rate takes over
item.description:
A hold was expected, so it should leave the yuan and Chinese bond markets little changed. The five respondents who expected a cut show that easing talk is building, which keeps attention on the PBoC’s next steps outside the LPR, such as reserve requirement cuts or targeted lending. Weak October activity data and a hawkish Fed narrow the room for rate cuts, since a lower rate would widen the gap with the US and add pressure to the yuan. For Asian equities, already under pressure from today’s chip selloff, the decision offers no fresh support.

Newswire cut: China kept its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and five-year at 3.5% for an 18th straight month, as expected by most. The LPR still prices most loans and mortgages, but the PBoC’s main signal is now its 1.25% overnight reverse repo rate.

One-line wrap: China’s lending benchmarks held steady again, a reminder that the LPR now follows Beijing’s policy signals rather than setting them.

Summary:

  • China held its one-year LPR at 3.0% and five-year LPR at 3.5%, an 18th consecutive month unchanged
  • 23 of 28 participants in a Reuters survey expected a hold, while five forecast a cut
  • The one-year rate is the benchmark for most corporate and household loans, and the five-year rate anchors mortgages
  • The LPR follows the PBoC’s policy operations rather than signalling policy itself
  • Since November 2, overnight reverse repo operations at 1.25% have been the PBoC’s main daily operation, replacing the seven-day repo
  • The PBoC plans to let strong companies price loans off the overnight rate, further reducing the LPR’s role

China left its benchmark lending rates unchanged for an 18th consecutive month on Friday. The one-year loan prime rate stayed at 3.0% and the five-year rate at 3.5%, in line with expectations from most market participants.

A Reuters survey of 28 respondents had found 23 expecting no change. Five forecast a cut to one or both rates, the first break from unanimous hold calls in recent months. That minority view reflected signs of renewed weakness in October, with factory output slowing and consumption subdued. Citigroup had described a November cut as implausible and expects rates to stay on hold through the rest of 2026, followed by two 10 basis point cuts in 2027.

What the LPR is

The loan prime rate is a benchmark lending rate set once a month. Twenty designated commercial banks submit quotes to the People’s Bank of China, and the published rate is meant to reflect what banks charge their most creditworthy borrowers. Other loans are priced as a spread above it.

What the two rates are used for

The one-year LPR is the reference for most corporate and household loans, including working capital lending to businesses. The five-year LPR is the main benchmark for mortgages, which makes it the rate to watch for any support aimed at the property sector.

Why it matters less than it used to

The LPR is not the PBoC’s policy rate. Banks set their quotes based on the central bank’s own operations, so the LPR tends to follow policy moves rather than signal them. For years, the medium-term lending facility played that anchoring role. In 2024 the PBoC made the seven-day reverse repo rate its main policy rate, most recently at 1.40%.

The bank has now gone a step further. From November 2, overnight reverse repo operations at 1.25% became the PBoC’s main daily operation, with seven-day operations kept as a liquidity tool used as needed. Governor Pan Gongsheng said in October that the interbank overnight repo rate had effectively become the central bank’s target. Analysts stress the switch is a reform rather than a rate cut, even though it lowered the floor of the rate framework by 15 basis points.

The PBoC also plans to let financially strong companies price loans off the overnight rate rather than the LPR. Over time, that would weaken the LPR’s role even in its core job of pricing bank loans.

For markets, that means a monthly LPR hold tells investors little on its own. Any shift in China’s policy stance is now more likely to show up first in the overnight rate, in reserve requirement changes or in targeted lending tools, with the LPR following later.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nikkei slides 4.5% and KOSPI tumbles as Wall Street’s AI reversal hits Asian chipmakers
item.description:
The selloff is concentrated in the AI supply chain, so chip-heavy indices like the Nikkei, the KOSPI and Taiwan’s market are the most exposed if US tech fails to steady. With Tokyo shut until Tuesday, Japanese exposure is likely to be hedged through Nikkei futures trading offshore, which could amplify moves. Risk-off flows can briefly support the yen, though the Fed-BoJ rate gap limits how far that goes. For broader sentiment, US futures in the Asian session and the Nasdaq’s next close are the tells.

---

Thursday:

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 19 Nov Inflation worries sink stocks

---

Wall Street’s whiplash session hit Asia’s AI darlings hardest, and a three-day weekend in Japan gave Tokyo investors one more reason to sell first.

Summary:

  • The Nikkei fell as much as 4.5%, dropping below 57,000 to a two-week low
  • Topix -2.7%
  • South Korea’s KOSPI fell more than 4% in early trade
  • The Nasdaq Composite swung from a gain of over 2% to a loss of over 2% as AI and chip stocks were sold
  • Anthropic’s record fundraising and Nasdaq debut failed to lift tech, with some investors citing selling in other assets to buy the shares
  • Advantest, SoftBank Group and Kioxia led Tokyo’s declines, and SK Hynix and Samsung each fell more than 5%
  • Japan’s markets are closed on Monday for a holiday, adding to risk aversion

Japanese and South Korean stocks tumbled on Friday as a sharp reversal in US technology shares spilled into Asia, hitting the region’s AI and semiconductor names hardest. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell as much as 4.5%, dropping below 57,000 to a two-week low, while South Korea’s KOSPI slid more than 4% in early trade.

The selling followed a volatile session on Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite swung from a gain of more than 2% to a loss of more than 2%, a reversal of over four percentage points in a single day. The move came as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut after a record-sized fundraising, and the listing failed to lift the wider technology sector. Some investors pointed to selling in other holdings to raise cash for Anthropic shares, a rotation that may have drained money from established AI names.

In Tokyo, chip-testing equipment maker Advantest, SoftBank Group and memory chipmaker Kioxia led the declines. In Seoul, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics each fell more than 5%. All four have been among the biggest beneficiaries of AI-related spending, which leaves them exposed when sentiment toward the theme turns.

Timing added to the pressure in Japan. Monday is a public holiday, so Tokyo markets are closed for three days, and investors appeared reluctant to hold risk over a long weekend in a market this volatile.

The broader backdrop has been difficult for high-valuation technology stocks. US Treasury yields are holding above 5% as markets price further Federal Reserve hikes, with several major banks now expecting moves in December, January and March. Higher yields reduce the present value of future earnings, which weighs most on growth-oriented sectors such as AI and semiconductors. Questions over the payback on AI investment have also grown, with UBS downgrading global equities to Neutral in its 2027 outlook and flagging concentration and AI execution risks.

For now, the moves look like a sentiment-driven selloff rather than a reaction to any single piece of company news. How US futures trade through the Asian session, and whether the Nasdaq can stabilise on Friday, will set the tone for Seoul and for Tokyo when it reopens on Tuesday.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan CPI misses on all three measures, but core stays above 2% ahead of a BoJ hike call
item.description:
The misses take a little edge off December hike pricing, but not enough to change the base case after Ueda’s hawkish remarks on Thursday. A slower underlying gauge leaves the yen with less support than it needed near 160, so the burden falls on intervention warnings rather than rate expectations. JGB yields may ease at the front end, but producer prices running at 7.1% keep the inflation pipeline full. With energy a key driver, oil remains a swing factor for whether underlying inflation turns back up as some economists expect.

----

The data post earlier:

  • Japan inflation picks up less than forecast as core-core slows to 2.2%

Japan’s inflation missed forecasts across the board but stayed above target, leaving the BoJ’s December hike intact and the yen still looking for support near 160.

Summary:

  • Core CPI (excluding fresh food) rose 2.2% y/y in October, against a 2.3% forecast and 2.1% in September
  • Headline CPI rose to 2.3% from 2.1%, below the 2.5% forecast
  • The index excluding fresh food and fuel slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, against a 2.3% forecast
  • Core inflation has exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target for a second straight month
  • 86% of economists polled expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, and one research house sees 2.5% by mid-2027
  • The BoJ’s policy rate is 1.25% after hikes in June and September

Japan’s core inflation rate picked up in October and stayed above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for a second straight month, although every major measure came in below forecasts. The result does little to change expectations that the BoJ will raise rates at its December meeting.

The core consumer price index, which excludes fresh food, rose 2.2% from a year earlier, below the median forecast of 2.3% but up from 2.1% in September. Headline inflation rose to 2.3% from 2.1%, short of the 2.5% expected. The index that excludes both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressure, slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, against a forecast of 2.3%.

That last reading is the one that gives doves something to point to. A slowdown in underlying inflation would normally argue for patience. But the gauge is still above target, and some economists expect it to accelerate sharply in the coming months as companies continue to pass on rising raw material costs. One research house now expects the BoJ to lift its policy rate to 2.5% by the middle of next year, well beyond current market pricing.

Cost pressures in the pipeline support that view. Japan’s producer prices rose 7.1% year on year in October, ahead of forecasts. Oil, chemicals, steel and utilities drove the rise, and a weak yen lifted import costs. Energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict have been a major driver of the pickup in consumer prices this year.

The BoJ’s policy rate stands at 1.25% after hikes in June and September, a faster pace than its roughly twice-yearly moves in 2024 and 2025. It held rates steady in October. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be the third increase this year. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative. He also flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the target.

There are offsetting concerns. The economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter, and the yen is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention this year. With the Fed also hiking, a December BoJ move may do little to narrow the rate gap that has kept pressure on the yen.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6731 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold slides toward $3,600 as sellers press on, but UBS upgrades it and still sees $5,000
item.description:
UBS’s upgrade gives longer-term buyers a reason to look at gold at these levels. But the near-term flow still belongs to rates, and nothing in the call changes the picture before the December 9 Fed decision. The low $3,600s are now being tested, and a clean break would leave the market with little obvious support until the high $3,500s. A short-covering bounce is possible if US data soften or the dollar pauses, but rallies are likely to meet selling while three-hike forecasts keep spreading.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit

---

Gold keeps falling on Fed hike bets, while UBS says the wait for a recovery is getting longer but the case for owning it at these prices is getting stronger.

Summary:

  • Gold has slipped to around $3,606, roughly 35% below January’s record, as hawkish Fed expectations, 5% Treasury yields and a firm dollar weigh
  • UBS has upgraded gold to Attractive in its Year Ahead 2027 outlook, forecasting $5,000 an ounce by December 2027
  • It cites structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields, with bond yields seen declining modestly later in 2027
  • The bank ranks bonds and commodities above equities, which it downgraded to Neutral, with cash least preferred
  • UBS’s $5,000 target has slipped from the first half of 2027 to the fourth quarter as the Fed turned more hawkish
  • It sees oil supported in the first half and names copper its preferred industrial metal

Gold is under heavy selling pressure again, slipping to around $3,606 an ounce in Asian trade and extending a slide that has taken it roughly 35% below its January record. The pressure is coming from the same place as all year: expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep raising rates. J.P. Morgan became the latest major bank on Thursday to forecast hikes in December, January and March. Treasury yields above 5% and a firm dollar continue to raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no income.

Against that backdrop, UBS has moved the other way. In its Year Ahead 2027 outlook, titled “Sustaining resilience,” the bank has upgraded gold to Attractive. It argues that structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields should support a recovery toward $5,000 an ounce by December 2027, which would be a gain of close to 40% from current levels.

The upgrade is part of a broader shift in UBS’s asset allocation. The bank now sees the most favourable risk-reward in bonds and commodities, followed by equities, with cash its least preferred asset class, and it has downgraded global equities to Neutral. It describes commodities as a way to protect portfolios against geopolitical disruption, inflation and constrained supply, with gold at the centre of that view.

UBS’s path to $5,000 has lengthened as the Fed has turned more hawkish. In August, the bank expected gold to reach $5,000 in the first half of 2027. As recently as October, its chief investment office saw $5,400 by September 2027. Earlier this week it pushed the $5,000 level back to the final quarter of 2027. The new outlook keeps that target but adds conviction through the upgrade. In effect, UBS is arguing that the wait may be longer, but the case is stronger at today’s prices.

The key condition is real yields. UBS expects easing inflation to allow bond yields to decline modestly later in 2027, and its chief investment office has forecast Fed hikes in December and March before that relief arrives. That sequencing explains the gap between the price and the forecast. Until real yields turn, the structural buyers UBS is counting on, chiefly central banks, are more likely to slow gold’s decline than reverse it.

Elsewhere in commodities, UBS expects oil to remain supported in the first half of 2027 and names copper as its preferred industrial metal, citing demand from electrification, power networks, data centres and AI infrastructure.

The call puts UBS among the more constructive major banks on gold, alongside Morgan Stanley at $5,250 for the fourth quarter of 2027 and ahead of Goldman Sachs at $4,650 for the end of next year. All three see higher prices from here. None sees a quick turn while the Fed is still hiking. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Paulson keeps quiet on December, says October’s pause was never meant as a stop
item.description:
With no fresh policy signal, the speech is unlikely to move rate pricing, and a quarter-point December hike remains the strong favourite. Her “pause was not a stop” framing supports the view that the hiking cycle runs into 2027, which keeps front-end Treasury yields and the dollar supported. Her three triggers for faster hikes give traders a checklist for the 4 December payrolls report and other data before the meeting: inflation expectations, wage growth and underlying inflation. An upside surprise on wages or expectations would strengthen the case for the larger move that Waller has floated.

---

Earlier:

  • JPMorgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call

---

Paulson argues the Fed should need to say less if markets understand it, and her policy view hasn’t changed: gradual hikes, with three clear reasons to go faster.

Summary:

  • Philadelphia Fed President Paulson offered no comment on the near-term rate outlook in a speech in New York
  • She said shared understanding of the Fed’s reaction function matters more than explicit forward guidance, which she said is less valuable in normal times
  • She said October’s hold after the September hike was not mistaken for the end of tightening because markets still expected more
  • On November 10 she backed further gradual hikes, saying policy needs to be somewhat restrictive
  • She named three triggers for faster action: rising inflation expectations, building wage pressures and higher underlying inflation
  • Markets widely expect a quarter-point hike to 4.00% to 4.25% at the December 8 to 9 meeting

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson stayed away from any near-term guidance on interest rates on Thursday. In a speech in New York, she argued that the Fed communicates best when the public understands how it thinks, not when officials spell out what comes next. With no fresh steer ahead of the December 8 to 9 meeting, her policy views from earlier this month remain the best guide to how she is likely to vote.

Speaking to the Money Marketeers of New York University, Paulson said understanding matters more than the particular ways the Fed communicates. If markets grasp the Fed’s reaction function, she argued, officials need to say less each time new data arrive, and policy can stay steady and largely predictable. She said the value of rate-path guidance depends on circumstances and is less useful in normal times, though Fed communications should still be clear about officials’ views.

She pointed to October as an example. The Fed held rates steady after hiking in September, but markets still expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind. In her words, shared understanding allowed policy to move deliberately, “without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop.” That was the closest she came to a signal: the October hold was a breather, not the end of the cycle.

Her remarks fit a wider debate inside the Fed. Under Chair Kevin Warsh, the central bank has shortened its policy statement and set up a task force on communications. Warsh himself has largely stepped back from giving rate guidance, even as many other officials continue to share their views.

Paulson had already shared hers. In a speech on November 10, she said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to 2% and that further gradual rate hikes seemed appropriate. She judged underlying inflation to be stuck between 2.5% and 3%. She also named three developments that would lead her to favour moving faster: inflation expectations drifting higher, wage pressures building, or underlying inflation rising. At the same time, she flagged that recent swings in stocks and oil could make consumer spending less durable than expected, one reason she prefers a gradual pace.

Read together, the two speeches point the same way. Paulson is a voter this year, and nothing in either speech suggests she would resist the quarter-point hike in December that markets widely expect, which would lift the target range to 4.00% to 4.25%. Thursday’s message adds that a slower pace should not be mistaken for a softer resolve.

item.title: 11-day Bitcoin redemption freeze: the risk hiding inside BTC-backed tokens
item.description:
At around 4,185 tokens, tBTC is far too small to move the BTC price, and the pause caused no visible spillover into spot Bitcoin, ETH or crypto equities. The pressure fell on DeFi lending. With redemption shut, liquidators taking tBTC collateral on Aave couldn’t fall back on redemption arbitrage, so they carried price and timing risk until they found a buyer. WBTC, cbBTC and other Bitcoin-backed tokens also depend on a bridge or custodian to keep minting and redemption open. Risk teams may now price that dependency into collateral settings more explicitly.

---

It was a heavy day for crypto:

  • Ethereum consolidates around recent lows

---

Threshold never ran short of Bitcoin, but for 11 days its token holders couldn’t get any of it back.

Summary:

  • Threshold Network suspended tBTC redemptions from Oct. 30 to Nov. 10. Its Nov. 18 post-mortem calls it an operational and security failure, not a reserve shortfall.
  • Bridge wallets held about 4,320 BTC against roughly 4,185 tBTC in circulation, a surplus of around 135 BTC.
  • There were two causes: a fault in how the bridge accounted for deposits, and a security issue tied to a Linux kernel flaw that took some signing operators offline. Each wallet needs a majority of its signers to move funds.
  • The Council restored Bitcoin proof submissions on Nov. 7. The app reopened at about 03:00 UTC on Nov. 10.
  • A review of 57 wallet addresses matched 31 redemption payouts to bridge proofs and found no unexplained outflows.
  • Aave froze its tBTC reserve on Ethereum V3 Core on Oct. 31. The reserve held about $136 million at the start of the freeze and about $120 million later.

Threshold Network kept tBTC holders from swapping their tokens back into native Bitcoin for 11 days, from Oct. 30 to Nov. 10, even though its bridge wallets held more Bitcoin than the tokens it had issued. The project’s post-mortem, published on Nov. 18, describes an operational and security failure rather than a shortfall in reserves.

On Oct. 31, Threshold reported roughly 4,320 BTC in its bridge wallets against about 4,185 tBTC in circulation, a cushion of around 135 BTC. That surplus did not help anyone who wanted out. The app stopped accepting redemption requests after unexpected bridge activity raised security concerns, and two separate problems then kept it shut.

The first was a fault in how the bridge accounted for incoming Bitcoin deposits, which the team said it identified before the suspension. The second was a security issue, linked in earlier updates to a critical Linux kernel flaw, that forced some of the node operators who sign Bitcoin transactions to patch their servers or take them offline. Because every bridge wallet needs signatures from more than half of its designated signers, withdrawals could not move until enough operators returned. Permission to submit Bitcoin proofs, which the bridge uses to verify deposits and redemption payouts, was also suspended, blocking the process at a second point.

Threshold said it fixed the accounting issue and upgraded the bridge before its Council restored proof submissions on Nov. 7. The app reopened at around 03:00 UTC on Nov. 10. A review of 57 registered wallet addresses and the bridge contracts, covering Oct. 25 to Nov. 12, matched 31 Bitcoin redemption payouts to their bridge proofs and found no unexplained outflows. Separately, one operator reported an unrelated infrastructure incident in which about 0.5 ETH left the Ethereum account it used for tBTC fees.

The episode spilled into lending. Aave froze its tBTC reserve on the Ethereum V3 Core market on Oct. 31, blocking new deposits and borrowing against the token while still allowing repayments, withdrawals and liquidations. The reserve held about $136 million when the freeze began and around $120 million by the time the bridge restarted.

The wider point for anyone holding Bitcoin in token form is that reserves and redemption are separate promises. A proof-of-reserves snapshot can show the coins exist, but getting them back depends on signers, software and governance all working at once. Readers should watch whether Aave lifts its reserve freeze, whether tBTC keeps trading close to Bitcoin now redemptions are open, and whether other Bitcoin-backed tokens publish clearer plans for keeping exits open during security emergencies. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Euro breaks below $1.10 as French election risk builds; three banks see $1.08 next
item.description:
With short positioning this stretched, the euro is vulnerable to sharp short-covering rallies even if the trend stays lower. A credible French budget or a soft US inflation reading would be the likeliest triggers. On the downside, the $1.08 to $1.09 area is the next focus, where the bank forecasts and options-market risk sit. The spread between French and German bonds is the gauge to watch: if it stays contained, the move remains mainly a dollar story, and if it widens, the French element takes over. A firm dollar also keeps USD/JPY pressing against Tokyo’s intervention zone near 160.

---

The euro is caught between French politics and a hawkish Fed, and forecasters see $1.08 next, though positioning is now crowded enough to make the next bounce a sharp one.

Summary:

  • EUR/USD has fallen below $1.10 to an 18-month low, about 6% lower since late August
  • Speculative bets against the euro are the largest in more than six years
  • Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank and another major European bank forecast $1.08 next year
  • Morgan Stanley expects French election risk to weigh, with the first round in April and a possible run-off in May
  • It sees the Fed hiking into early 2027 and no US cuts until 2028, supporting the dollar even as stocks rally
  • Some analysts argue the slide is mainly about the dollar rather than France, as the euro is not weak across the board

The euro has slipped below $1.10 against the dollar for the first time in about 18 months, and the market is positioning for further losses. The single currency is down roughly 6% since late August, and speculative bets against it are at their heaviest in more than six years. Weeks of political unrest in France and doubts over the government’s ability to pass a budget have added a home-grown problem to a dollar that was already firm.

Forecasters see more downside ahead. Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank, along with another major European lender, expect EUR/USD to fall to $1.08 next year. Morgan Stanley’s 2027 outlook, covered earlier this week, sees the euro as the weak side of the trade. It expects political risk premium to build ahead of the French presidential election, with the first round due in April and a run-off in May if no candidate wins outright.

The bank’s argument goes further than France. Its strategists expect developed-market central banks to keep raising rates into early 2027. Fed tightening keeps US Treasury yields elevated, and they do not see the first US rate cuts until 2028. In that setting, they expect the dollar to rally modestly, supported by confidence in US growth and wider rate differentials. They also expect a strong year for equities, with an 8,700 target for the S&P 500. That challenges the usual pattern in which risk-on markets weigh on the dollar. If US growth stays strong, stocks and the dollar can rise together, leaving the euro the more vulnerable currency.

Not everyone reads the euro’s slide as a French story. Some analysts point out that the euro has weakened against the dollar, yen and sterling but not across the board, and that a genuine flight from French risk would normally show up as wider French bond spreads against Germany. On that view, the move is mostly about US rates. Options markets also suggest investors have not yet rushed to buy protection against a much deeper fall. Some strategists see risks skewed only modestly lower, toward the high $1.08s.

The near-term drivers line up on the dollar’s side. US policymakers are signalling further hikes ahead of the December 8 to 9 Fed meeting, and several major banks now expect moves in December, January and March. For the euro, the French budget process and the build-up to the spring election are the main domestic risks. With positioning already stretched, though, any sign of fiscal progress in Paris or a softer US inflation reading could trigger a sharp bounce as shorts are covered. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Barclays: Back-to-back Fed hikes give the dollar staying power that a jumbo 50bp move wouldn’t
item.description:
The focus for the dollar shifts from how big the December hike will be to how long the hiking continues. That leans toward front-end Treasury yields staying high into the first quarter. It’s a constructive backdrop for the dollar against lower-yielding currencies, although intervention risk near 160 limits the upside in USD/JPY. Gold faces the same headwind it has struggled with all year, as longer-lasting high US rates raise the cost of holding it. Freight and diesel costs are a direct channel from oil to US core inflation, so oil prices now feed straight into Fed pricing.

---

Barclays says the dollar’s strength comes from how long the Fed keeps hiking, not how big any single move is, and two quarter-point steps do that job better than one jumbo hike.

Summary:

  • Barclays forecasts 25 basis point Fed hikes in December and January, taking the target range to 4.25% to 4.50%
  • It does not expect the 50 basis point December move Governor Waller has suggested officials should consider
  • The bank argues two consecutive hikes would keep US rates higher for longer and support the dollar more durably than one jumbo hike
  • October CPI rose 0.4% on the month against 0.3% expected, and Barclays sees energy, diesel and freight costs spreading into core goods prices
  • J.P. Morgan, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America expect three hikes, putting Barclays mid-range among tier-one forecasters

Barclays says the case for a stronger dollar does not depend on the Federal Reserve delivering a half-point hike in December. In its view, two consecutive quarter-point moves would do more for the currency over time, keeping US rates higher for longer rather than front-loading the tightening in a single step.

The bank’s economists forecast 25 basis point hikes at both the December 8 to 9 and January 26 to 27 meetings. That would lift the federal funds target range from 3.75% to 4.00% now to 4.25% to 4.50% early next year. Barclays does not expect the 50 basis point move that Governor Christopher Waller has argued officials should consider in December. Futures still show a quarter-point December hike as the overwhelming favourite.

The forecast is not new, but Barclays has grown more confident in it. The bank first added a January hike in mid-October, after previously expecting the Fed to stop in December. October’s inflation figures then delivered a run of upside surprises, with headline CPI rising 0.4% on the month against expectations of 0.3%. Barclays says diesel and energy costs are now passing through into a widening set of core categories, with higher freight costs reaching consumer goods. That broadening is the key point. An inflation shock that spreads beyond fuel is harder for the Fed to look through, which argues for sustained tightening rather than one dramatic move.

Barclays has also said that limited prospects for much lower oil prices, solid economic data and hawkish comments from officials all point to more hikes in the near term. That makes the path of crude a direct input into its rate and currency views.

The call puts Barclays in the middle of the tier-one pack. J.P. Morgan, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America expect three consecutive hikes, adding March to the December and January moves, while Goldman Sachs sees a December hike followed by another in March. What unites most of them is the view that the cycle does not end in December, and Barclays sees that as the most supportive part of the story for the dollar.

The dollar index is already near its highest in about 19 months, so the argument is about how durable that strength is rather than whether it exists. A single jumbo hike could be read as the Fed catching up and then stopping. A steady sequence of hikes into 2027 keeps the rate gap with other major economies wider for longer. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit
item.description:
Gold now trades below most major bank year-end targets, leaving it oversold on fundamentals but without a catalyst to turn it. With the $3,700 handle gone, traders are looking for support in the low $3,600s and high $3,500s, and a clean break would invite more momentum selling. The December 9 Fed decision is the main event risk: a 50 basis point hike or a higher dot plot would extend losses, while any hint the cycle is near its end could spark a sharp short-covering bounce. Miners are still far above record production costs, so margins can absorb further weakness, and supply is unlikely to tighten from producers cutting output.

---

Gold’s sellers have rates, yields and the dollar on their side, while its buyers are central banks and long-term investors who are patient but too slow to stop the slide.

Summary:

  • Gold has slumped to around $3,625, about 35% below its late-January record near $5,590
  • Selling themes: a Fed on a hiking path, US yields above 5%, a firm dollar, US fund outflows, weak retail demand in India and weaker jewellery buying in China, and bank forecast cuts
  • Geopolitics has worked against gold: escalation lifts oil, inflation and Fed hike expectations
  • Buying themes: central bank purchases of about 321 tonnes in Q3, record global ETF holdings, and record Chinese bar and coin demand year to date
  • Major bank targets remain well above spot, with Goldman Sachs at $4,650 and Morgan Stanley at $5,250 for late 2027
  • The December 9 Fed decision is the next key test

Gold has slumped to around $3,625 an ounce, about 35% below its record near $5,590 set in late January. Sellers have been in control for most of the year, and the past week has brought some of the heaviest losses yet. The bull case has not disappeared, but it now rests on slower-moving, structural buyers, while the forces pushing prices down are immediate and tied to rates. Here is how the two sides line up.

Selling theme 1: A Fed that keeps hiking

The biggest weight on gold is the Federal Reserve. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect further hikes, markets see a December move as close to certain, and J.P. Morgan now forecasts hikes in December, January and March. Each step raises the cost of holding a metal that pays no yield. Hawkish signals from the Fed drove gold’s 3% slide this week, its steepest in some time.

Selling theme 2: Yields above 5% and a firm dollar

The US 10-year Treasury yield is holding above 5%, and the dollar index is near its highest in about 19 months. Together they give investors a competitive return elsewhere and make gold more expensive for buyers outside the US.

Selling theme 3: Geopolitics works against gold, not for it

Through the Middle East conflict, gold has not behaved as a haven. Escalation pushes oil higher, oil feeds inflation, and inflation feeds expectations of further Fed hikes and higher yields. Renewed US-Iran strikes this month brought no safe-haven buying, with rates outweighing geopolitics.

Selling theme 4: US fund selling and a weaker retail bid

The outflows are concentrated in the US. North America was the only region with gold ETF outflows in October, and retail bar and coin demand fell about a fifth year on year in the third quarter. The weakness was most visible in Asia’s two biggest consumer markets. Indian bar and coin buying fell about 40%, accounting for most of the global drop, and jewellery demand in both China and India fell by around a fifth as high prices put shoppers off. Silver, down more than 60% from its peak, shows how hard forced selling has hit the wider precious metals complex.

Selling theme 5: Forecast cuts and broken support

Big banks have been lowering their numbers. Goldman Sachs has cut its outlook twice in less than a month, most recently trimming its end-2027 target to $4,650 from $4,800 after earlier reducing it from $5,400. On the charts, the break below $3,700 removed a closely watched level, and some analysts see the next support areas in the high $3,500s to mid-$3,600s.

Buying theme 1: Central banks are still accumulating

The strongest argument for the bulls is official-sector demand. Central banks bought about 321 tonnes in the third quarter, up more than 40% on a year earlier. Goldman Sachs assumes roughly 60 tonnes a month of central bank buying, against about 17 tonnes before 2022, and sees that as the main pillar of its forecast. These purchases tend to show up in data with a lag, so they offer little near-term support for prices.

Buying theme 2: Outside the US, investors are still adding

Global gold ETF holdings reached a record near 4,256 tonnes in October, helped by inflows from European funds. Chinese retail investors have also stayed committed: bar and coin demand in China rose 7% year on year in the third quarter, and its year-to-date total is the highest on record. That suggests the selling is regional rather than a wholesale exit from gold.

Buying theme 3: Long-run targets sit well above spot

Even after the cuts, major bank forecasts are well above the current price. Goldman Sachs sees $4,650 by the end of 2027, Morgan Stanley targets $5,250 for the fourth quarter of 2027, and Deutsche Bank sees a conditional debasement case for 2027 to 2028 if the Fed eventually eases or financial repression returns. The gap between those targets largely reflects different assumptions about rates and official buying.

Buying theme 4: The eventual turn in the rate cycle

Gold’s best route back is the end of the hiking cycle. Goldman Sachs’s base case has the Fed cutting from the second half of 2027. Once markets start pricing an end to tightening, the main source of selling pressure would ease.

Who has the upper hand

For now, the sellers. The forces pushing gold lower are fast-moving and tied to rates, while the buyers are patient, price-insensitive and slow to show up in the data. The next key test is the December 9 Fed decision and its projections, which will show how far into 2027 officials expect to keep hiking. Until the rate outlook turns, central bank demand looks more likely to slow the decline than reverse it. 

Whaddaya call a kangaroo with no bounce?

item.title: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call

---

J.P. Morgan has dropped its “December and done” view: it now expects three straight hikes, with the Fed defending its credibility rather than reacting to a hot labour market.

Summary:

  • J.P. Morgan now forecasts 25 basis point Fed hikes in January and March 2027, on top of the December hike it already expected
  • Three hikes would take the federal funds range from 3.75% to 4.00% up to 4.50% to 4.75% by March
  • Its economists say the labour market has not been a source of inflation, and the hikes are about preserving credibility while there is no compelling case to pause
  • They argue the Fed under Chair Warsh lacks an overarching narrative, so policy is likely to react to each new data release
  • In early October the bank expected December to be the last hike, seeing inflation as driven mainly by supply shocks
  • Deutsche Bank and Bank of America also see three straight hikes, while Goldman Sachs and UBS expect a shorter path

J.P. Morgan has moved to a longer Fed tightening path, now forecasting quarter-point rate hikes in January and March 2027 on top of the December increase it already expected. If all three go ahead, the federal funds target range would rise from 3.75% to 4.00% now to 4.50% to 4.75% by March. The new path would mean hikes at the December 8 to 9, January 26 to 27 and March 16 to 17 meetings.

The bank’s economists, led by chief US economist Michael Feroli, said the extra hikes are not meant to weaken the labour market, which they argue has not been a source of inflation. The aim instead is to protect the Fed’s credibility when policymakers have no convincing reason to stop. In their view, sticky inflation keeps the case for further tightening alive.

The revision is a notable change of view. As recently as early October, J.P. Morgan expected December to be the last move of the cycle. It argued then that supply shocks were the main driver of inflation and would not justify a long campaign into 2027. Adding two more hikes suggests the bank no longer sees price pressure as a passing supply story.

The economists also raised a point about communication under Chair Kevin Warsh. They said the Fed has not set out an overarching narrative for its policy path, and without one, decisions are more likely to react to each new data release. In practice, that raises the stakes for every inflation release between now and March.

The call fits the tone of the Fed’s own minutes. The record of the October 27 to 28 meeting, released on Wednesday, showed almost all officials judged further hikes would likely be needed if the economy evolved as they expected. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee added to that on Thursday, saying that in his view a sizeable part of inflation comes from demand, not just oil and tariff shocks.

J.P. Morgan is not alone. Deutsche Bank and Bank of America also forecast hikes at three straight meetings, while Goldman Sachs and UBS expect a shorter path after December and some other forecasters see a longer pause. Markets price a quarter-point December hike as close to certain, with a small chance of a half-point move. The bigger question now is whether the cycle ends in December or runs well into 2027, and J.P. Morgan has clearly taken the second view. 

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More from Fed’s Goolsbee: AI boom a ‘pig through the python’ that risks overheating US economy
item.description:
Goolsbee’s remarks add a demand-side argument to a Fed debate already leaning toward hikes. Markets heavily favour a quarter-point move on December 9, and a voice outside the usual hawks warning of overheating supports front-end yields and the dollar. He says inflation is not just an oil and tariff story, so a pullback in crude would ease less of the pressure than traders might hope. His uncertainty about how banks would cope with an AI-led equity correction marks a tail risk for stocks that could quickly reverse the tightening narrative.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed's Goolsbee: Job market is stable, but inflation is "way higher" than Fed's 2% target
  • Fed’s Goolsbee says he sees no clear path back to 2% inflation

---

Goolsbee says the AI boom has become an inflation problem, with investment and stock market wealth pushing on an economy that may not have the room to absorb them.

Summary:

  • Chicago Fed President Goolsbee warned that the AI investment surge risks overheating the US economy and adding to inflation
  • He does not yet see inflation on a path back to 2%, calls it borderline disturbingly high and says the steepness of the rate path depends on that outlook
  • He says inflation reflects a sizeable demand component, not only oil and tariff shocks, and services inflation is key to telling the two apart
  • AI is affecting the economy through investment and wealth effects, and he says Anthropic’s record IPO raises questions about how shareholders will spend their gains
  • He is not worried about wages adding to inflation and sees consumer spending as broad-based and mostly funded by income growth
  • He is unsure how the financial sector would handle a major AI-related equity correction

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee warned on Thursday that the artificial intelligence boom is adding to the risk of the US economy overheating. Business investment at near-unprecedented levels may be more than the economy’s capacity can absorb, he argued. He compared the surge to a pig moving through a python and said he found it hard to see the AI boom as anything other than a contributor to overheating. He made the comments in a call with reporters on the day Anthropic set a record for an initial public offering.

Goolsbee’s central message was that he does not yet see inflation on a path back to the Fed’s 2% target. In his view, inflation has proved far more persistent than expected in 2025, and recent months have not brought good news. He called the level of inflation borderline disturbingly high and said how steep the rate path needs to be depends on whether inflation is seen returning to target.

He was explicit that the pressure is not only coming from supply shocks. Oil and tariffs have played a part, he said, but there is also a sizeable demand component. That is why he is watching services inflation closely, as a guide to whether price pressures come from demand or from costs such as energy.

He pointed to two channels through which AI is shaping the economy: investment, and the wealth effect from rising equity values. The Anthropic listing raises the question of how shareholders will spend their gains, he said, which could have a broader macroeconomic impact. He added that businesses widely acknowledge costs are rising, especially in construction and at firms competing with data centres for components.

Not every signal was hawkish. Goolsbee said he is not concerned about wages pushing up inflation at this point. He described consumer spending as broad-based and financed mostly by income growth. He was less certain about the risks around equities. It is unclear how the financial sector would fare in a major AI-related stock correction, he said, and he is unsure whether fallout from the US midterm elections will slow the data centre buildout or leave a lasting mark on share prices. He also said greater openness about monetary policy has been productive for the Fed and for the world.

The remarks add a new strand to the Fed’s debate ahead of the December 8 to 9 meeting, where hikes are the focus. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all participants saw further hikes as likely appropriate, and markets lean heavily toward a quarter-point rise from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range. Goolsbee, a 2027 voter, did not commit to the size of a December move in the remarks available. But by framing AI as a demand-side inflation risk, he gives the hawks another argument. If services inflation and investment spending stay hot into early 2027, a longer tightening cycle looks more likely than a quick finish. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, November 20, 2026: Fed's Paulson, Japan CPI and China’s LPR
item.description:
USD/JPY near 160 is where today’s events meet. A firm Japan CPI would support the yen at the margin, but a Fed that is also hiking limits how far the rate gap can narrow, and intervention warnings near 160 cap the upside. If Paulson sounds open to a 50 basis point move rather than gradual steps, front-end Treasury yields and the dollar would likely rise. Energy is a big part of Japan’s inflation pickup, so oil prices feed straight into the BoJ’s thinking. A hold on the LPR should barely move the yuan, while a surprise cut would stand out given the overnight-rate overhaul.

Two hawkish central banks get fresh tests in the Asian session, while China’s loan prime rate holds as a benchmark the PBoC has quietly moved past.

Summary:

  • Philadelphia Fed President Paulson, a 2026 voter, speaks at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern) in New York, ahead of the December 8 to 9 FOMC meeting
  • She recently backed further gradual hikes and said she would move faster if inflation expectations, wages or underlying inflation rise
  • Japan’s October core CPI is expected at 2.3%, up from 2.1%, also at 23:30 GMT
  • BoJ Governor Ueda said on Thursday the bank expects to keep raising rates, and 86% of economists polled see a hike to 1.50% on December 17 to 18
  • China’s one-year and five-year LPRs are expected to hold at 3.0% and 3.5% at 01:15 GMT, though five of 28 survey respondents see a cut
  • The PBoC made overnight reverse repo operations at 1.25% its main daily operation from November 2, further reducing the LPR’s role as a policy signal

The Asian session brings a cluster of events that will test how firmly markets are leaning into a global tightening story. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson speaks late in the US day, Japan’s national inflation figures for October are released at the same time, and China’s monthly loan prime rate fixing follows early in the session. The first two fit squarely into a hawkish narrative on both sides of the Pacific. The third is a largely procedural event that matters less than it used to.

Fed’s Paulson: a 2026 voter on a committee leaning toward hikes

Paulson is due to speak at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern) at a Money Marketeers of New York University dinner in New York. She is scheduled to address communications and monetary policy, and a speech text and a question-and-answer session are expected. As a 2026 FOMC voter, her views carry weight heading into the December 8 to 9 meeting, with the decision due on December 9.

Her recent record is clear. In a speech earlier this month she said further gradual rate increases seemed appropriate. Policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to get inflation back to 2%, she said, and underlying inflation appears stuck between 2.5% and 3%. She would favour moving faster if inflation expectations drift higher, wage pressures build or underlying inflation rises. She backed the September hike and the October hold.

The backdrop has grown more hawkish since then. Minutes of the October 27 to 28 meeting, released on Wednesday, showed nearly all participants judged that further increases in the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate in the coming months. Governor Christopher Waller believes officials should consider a half-point move in December, arguing that recent inflation is heading the wrong way. With the target range at 3.75% to 4.00%, markets lean heavily toward a quarter-point hike. Deutsche Bank expects hikes in December, January and March, while Citigroup sees a 25 basis point move in December with a higher risk of 50.

The key question for Paulson is whether she sticks with “gradual” or shows any openness to the larger step Waller has floated. Any change in how she talks about the pace would make the headline.

Japan’s October CPI: inflation data ahead of a likely BoJ hike

Japan’s national CPI for October is due at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern). The consensus for the core measure, which excludes fresh food, is 2.3%, up from 2.1% in September. The prior headline reading was 2.1%, and the measure excluding both fresh food and energy was 2.4%. Economists have linked much of the recent pickup to higher energy costs from the Middle East conflict reaching household bills, while a weak yen has pushed up import prices.

The data arrive with the Bank of Japan in a hawkish mood. The policy rate is 1.25% after a hike in September, its highest in 31 years. On Thursday, Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative. He also flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be a third increase this year. Nearly 60% look for a further move to 1.75% by the end of March. Producer prices strengthened the case earlier this month, rising 7.1% y/y in October, ahead of forecasts.

There are complications. The economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter, and the yen is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention this year. A firm CPI reading would reinforce December hike pricing. A soft one would give doves a talking point, though probably not enough to derail the move given Ueda’s latest remarks.

PBoC loan prime rates: an 18th hold expected for a fading benchmark

China’s loan prime rates are due at 01:15 GMT (20:15 US Eastern). In a Reuters survey of 28 market participants, 23 expect the one-year LPR to hold at 3.0% and the five-year at 3.5%. That would be an 18th consecutive month unchanged. Five respondents see a cut to one or both rates, the first break from unanimous no-change forecasts in recent months. Citigroup analysts see a November cut as implausible and expect rates to stay on hold through 2026, followed by two 10 basis point cuts in 2027.

The LPR is compiled monthly from quotes submitted by 20 designated commercial banks. The one-year rate is the benchmark for most corporate and household loans. The five-year rate is the main reference for mortgage pricing, which makes it the rate to watch for any property support.

As a policy signal, though, the LPR has slipped down the rankings. The PBoC made the seven-day reverse repo its main policy rate in 2024 (most recently at 1.40%), and has now gone a step further. From November 2, overnight reverse repo operations (at 1.25%) became the central bank’s main daily operation, and seven-day operations are now a liquidity tool used as needed. Governor Pan Gongsheng had said in October that the interbank overnight repo rate had effectively become the PBoC’s target. The switch lowered the floor of the rate framework by 15 basis points, although analysts stress it is a reform rather than a rate cut. The PBoC also plans to let stronger firms price loans off the overnight rate instead of the LPR, which would weaken the LPR’s role further.

Also on the calendar

UK GfK consumer confidence for November is due at 00:01 GMT (19:01 US Eastern), expected at -22 from -24. New Zealand card spending follows at 02:00 GMT (21:00 US Eastern), and ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone speaks at 03:10 GMT (22:10 US Eastern).

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Goolsbee says he sees no clear path back to 2% inflation
item.description:
Goolsbee’s comments on inflation, interest rates and AI investment crossed the wires.

  • What is happening with services inflation is important in understanding whether price pressures stem from demand or things like energy costs.
  • Inflation has proven to be far more persistent than was thought in 2025, and data center demand and AI-related wealth impact is adding to it.
  • The steepness of the interest-rate path will be rooted in whether “borderline disturbingly high” inflation is seen returning to Fed’s 2% target.
  • Does not see at this point that inflation is on the path back to 2%. It is not just coming from oil and tariff shocks, but a sizable demand component.
  • Is not concerned about wages pressuring inflation at this point.
  • It has not been good news on inflation for the past few months.
  • Anthropic’s IPO raises the question of how stockholders will use that wealth. It could have a macroeconomic impact.
  • Artificial intelligence is influencing today’s economy through wealth impacts and investment.
  • There is widespread acknowledgment among businesses that costs are up, particularly among firms in construction or competing with data centers for components.
  • Is not sure if fallout from US midterm elections will include a slowdown in data-center buildout or have a lasting impact on equity prices.
  • More openness about monetary policy has been productive for the Fed and the world.
  • Consumer spending has been pretty broad-based, financed mostly out of income growth.
  • There is a high risk that economy’s capacity cannot handle the current “pig-through-the-python” level of business investment without overheating.
  • Not clear how financial sector would be impacted if there is a major correction in equities related to AI.

Analysis

The takeaway is hawkish. Goolsbee sees a sizable demand component to inflation, which makes it harder for the Fed to look through the recent price pressure. Businesses are already reporting higher costs where they compete with data centers for components, and he sees a risk that the economy has trouble absorbing the current pace of investment without overheating.

Services inflation is the barometer to watch. If it stays sticky even as energy pressures ease, that would strengthen the case that demand is keeping inflation elevated and give the Fed more reason to tighten. If services inflation cools, the case for a steeper rate path weakens.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUDUSD moves to a new low. Price action is ping ponging down and up and back down again.
item.description:
Australia’s October jobs report was considerably weaker than expected. Employment fell 43,500 against the 25,500 gain expected in our preview, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.9% versus 4.7% expected. September’s job loss was revised to 36,400 from 39,300, putting the two-month decline at nearly 80,000 jobs, the biggest in five years.

Part-time jobs accounted for most of the decline

  • Full-time employment fell 2,900. Part-time employment fell 40,600.
  • Participation fell to 66.6% from 66.8%, while the number of unemployed people still rose by 17,800. Hours worked fell 0.2%.
  • Youth unemployment rose to 11.3% from 11.1%, also the highest since October 2021.

The rise in unemployment alongside a drop in participation is the detail that stands out. A smaller share of Australians were working or looking for work, and even with that decline in participation, more people were unemployed. The ABS’s smoothed trend measure still showed a modest gain of 7,200 jobs, but trend unemployment also rose, to 4.8%.

The RBA has more reason to pause

The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% earlier this month and warned that inflation would stay elevated for longer. The jobs report strengthens the case for a hold on December 8. Reuters reported that traders unwound bets on further hikes and priced in roughly 45 basis points of easing by the end of 2027, about double what they had priced before the release

Technically, the price moved lower  but bounced before reversing to a new low.

The AUDUSD initially fell sharply from 0.67202 to near 0.6660 after the weaker-than-expected Australian jobs report. Buyers came back in and erased nearly the entire decline, taking the pair back toward the Asian session high at 0.6720 early in North American trading.

That rebound did not last. As U.S. stocks reversed their early gains, traders turned their attention back to U.S. inflation concerns and still-solid jobs data. Sellers took control again, retracing the entire bounce and extending the move to a new session low at 0.66562. The pair is trading at 0.66624 as the North American session winds down.

The 200-week moving average is the barometer

The session low at 0.66562 dipped just below the 200-week moving average at 0.66575. The price is back above it for now, putting the focus on where the pair closes the week. A weekly close below 0.66575 would give sellers more control and increase the potential for further downside.

If buyers can hold above that moving average and build on the bounce, the 100-week moving average at 0.67043 is the first key topside target. Getting back above it would give buyers more room to make a run at the session high near 0.6720.
